entries.sentence: Gout is an inflammatory arthritis caused by urate crystals in and around joints, and it causes sudden flares of severe pain and swelling.
entries.note: Search summary blends pages; page-level attribution uncertain. Summary said gout is inflammatory arthritis from urate crystals causing sudden flares of severe pain and swelling.

entries.sentence: The affected joint becomes hot and very tender, and the big toes, ankles, knees and fingers are the usual places.
entries.note: Summary: big toes, ankles, knees and fingers are usual sites; joint hot and very tender.

entries.sentence: Left untreated, an attack usually lasts about one to two weeks.
entries.note: NHS: an attack usually lasts 1 to 2 weeks if left untreated.

entries.sentence: If gout is not treated, future attacks may last even longer.
entries.note: NHS: without treatment future attacks may last even longer.

entries.sentence: Almost everyone with gout has further flares, and these usually come within a year.
entries.note: NHS inform per summary: almost everyone with gout has further flares, usually within a year.

entries.sentence: Over time the attacks can become more frequent and longer, which may lead to chronic gout with lumps of uric acid crystals called tophi.
entries.note: Search summary blends pages; page-level attribution uncertain. Summary from NHS-affiliated page: frequency and duration of acute attacks increase and lead to chronic gout with tophi.

entries.sentence: The severe pain can make everyday tasks and getting around difficult.
entries.note: Summary: severe pain makes everyday tasks and getting around difficult.

entries.sentence: At an appointment, a GP will usually ask about your symptoms and medical history and examine the affected joint.
entries.note: NHS: GP asks about symptoms and medical history and examines the area.

entries.sentence: They may also ask about your diet and whether anyone in your family has had gout.
entries.note: NHS: may ask about diet and family history of gout.

entries.sentence: A blood test for uric acid may be done, but the level in the blood often falls during a flare.
entries.note: Summary: urate level often falls during a flare; NICE says serum urate can read lower during a flare.

entries.sentence: Because of this, a GP may wait about four weeks after a flare before doing the test.
entries.note: Summary quoting NHS-affiliated text: GP may wait 4 weeks after a flare before the test.

entries.sentence: A normal result during a flare does not rule gout out.
entries.note: Summary of NICE: urate can read falsely low in a flare so normal does not rule gout out.

entries.sentence: When the diagnosis is uncertain, fluid can be taken from the joint and looked at under a microscope for crystals.
entries.note: Summary: joint aspiration and microscopy of synovial fluid when diagnosis uncertain.

entries.sentence: An ultrasound or a special CT scan can also check for crystal build-up in the joint.
entries.note: NIAMS: ultrasound or special CT can check for urate crystal buildup.

entries.sentence: If the picture is still unclear, a GP may refer you to a rheumatologist, a joint specialist, for further tests.
entries.note: Summary: if unclear, GP may refer to a rheumatologist and arrange further tests.

entries.sentence: Treatment has two parts: easing a flare, and preventing future flares.
entries.note: Summary: management covers flare treatment and long-term prevention (NICE ULT).

entries.sentence: NICE recommends an anti-inflammatory painkiller (an NSAID) or a short course of steroid tablets as the first choice for a flare.
entries.note: Summary of NICE: NSAIDs or short oral corticosteroid course first line.

entries.sentence: A steroid injection is an option when those medicines and colchicine cannot be used.
entries.note: Summary: corticosteroid injection an option when NSAIDs and colchicine cannot be used.

entries.sentence: Colchicine is another option, and NIAMS notes that it works best when it is started as soon as symptoms appear.
entries.note: Summary: NIAMS names colchicine as an option, works best when taken when symptoms first appear.

entries.sentence: NHS Inform advises starting medicine as early as possible, and it should begin to work within two or three days.
entries.note: Summary: start medication as early as possible; should begin to work within 2 or 3 days.

entries.sentence: Ice packs can also ease symptoms.
entries.note: Summary: ice packs can ease symptoms.

entries.sentence: For flares at night, Versus Arthritis suggests raising the joint on a cushion, using ice and keeping bedsheets off the sore area.
entries.note: Summary of Versus Arthritis: raise joint on cushion, ice, keep bedsheets off.

entries.sentence: NICE describes gout as a lifelong condition that benefits from long-term urate-lowering treatment, which aims to clear the urate crystals and prevent flares.
entries.note: Summary: NICE calls gout lifelong and benefits from long-term ULT to eliminate crystals and prevent flares.

entries.sentence: NICE says this treatment can also shrink tophi and prevent long-term joint damage.
entries.note: Summary: ULT can shrink tophi and prevent long-term joint damage.

entries.sentence: NHS Inform says lifelong treatment is usually needed.
entries.note: Summary: lifelong treatment usually required.

entries.sentence: Flares can increase when urate-lowering medicine is first started, so doctors may give another medicine alongside it for the first months.
entries.note: Search summary blends pages; page-level attribution uncertain. Summary: flares can increase on starting ULT; prophylaxis for months (from a drug label).

entries.sentence: NICE also notes that starting allopurinol gently and building up gradually causes fewer flares than a high start.
entries.note: Summary: starting at a higher amount can worsen flares more than starting low and increasing.

entries.sentence: NIAMS says lifestyle changes alone are not enough when flares are frequent or tophi are present, so medicine is the main approach.
entries.note: Summary: lifestyle alone not sufficient when flares frequent or tophi present; medication is main approach.

entries.sentence: Diet changes can still help alongside medicine.
entries.note: Summary: diet changes can help, but medication is the main approach.

entries.sentence: Versus Arthritis says heavy drinking, especially of beer and spirits, can raise urate levels and trigger attacks.
entries.note: Summary of VA: heavy drinking especially beer and spirits raises urate and triggers attacks.

entries.sentence: It says small amounts of wine do not appear to raise the risk, and it suggests spreading any drinking across the week.
entries.note: Summary: small amounts of wine don't appear to raise risk; spread units across week.

entries.sentence: It advises losing weight gradually, because crash diets can raise urate levels and losing too much weight too soon can trigger an attack.
entries.note: Summary: gradual loss; starvation diets raise urate; losing too much too soon can cause an attack.

entries.sentence: The NHS also advises avoiding crash diets and drinking plenty of fluids so that you do not get dehydrated.
entries.note: Summary quoting NHS: lose weight but avoid crash diets; drink plenty of fluids to avoid dehydration.

entries.sentence: Versus Arthritis suggests cutting down on sweetened soft drinks and says skimmed milk and low-fat yoghurt may help prevent attacks.
entries.note: Summary of VA: cut sweetened soft drinks; skimmed milk and low-fat yoghurt may help.

entries.sentence: The NHS and other sources also suggest limiting purine-rich foods such as red meat and seafood.
entries.note: Search summary blends pages; page-level attribution uncertain. Summary: NHS and others recommend limiting sugary drinks and purine-rich foods such as red meat and seafood.

entries.sentence: The NHS says vitamin C supplements may help a little, but you should talk to a GP first because they are not suitable for everyone.
entries.note: Summary quoting NHS: talk to GP before vitamin C supplements as not suitable for everyone; may help a little.

entries.sentence: Leaving gout untreated may cause lasting damage to the joints.
entries.note: NHS: leaving gout untreated may cause lasting damage to joints.

entries.sentence: Gout can also affect your mood, work and home life, and the pain can lead to feelings of depression or anxiety.
entries.note: Summary quoting NHS: gout can affect mood, work and home life; depression or anxiety.

entries.sentence: NIAMS lists care for related conditions, such as heart and kidney disease, as part of treatment.
entries.note: Summary: NIAMS lists care for related conditions such as heart and kidney disease.

entries.sentence: NHS sources describe gout as manageable, because medicines can help the pain and healthier lifestyle choices can help prevent future attacks.
entries.note: Summary: painkillers help pain and healthier lifestyle choices can prevent future attacks.

entries.sentence: See a GP at a routine appointment if you have symptoms of gout for the first time, or if you have gout and your usual treatments are not helping.
entries.note: NHS: see a GP if symptoms for the first time or usual treatments not helping.

entries.sentence: Get an urgent GP appointment or call NHS 111 if a swollen joint gets worse, or if you also have a high temperature of 38C or above, or feel sick or unable to eat.
entries.note: NHS: urgent GP or NHS 111 if swollen joint worse, fever 38C or above, or feel sick/unable to eat.

entries.sentence: These can be signs of an infection inside the joint, called septic arthritis.
entries.note: NHS: fever could mean infection inside the joint (septic arthritis).

entries.sentence: Left untreated, a gout attack usually lasts about one to two weeks.
entries.note: NHS: 1 to 2 weeks untreated.

entries.sentence: Without treatment, later attacks may last even longer.
entries.note: NHS: future attacks may last even longer.

entries.sentence: Medicine taken as soon as possible should start to work within about two days, according to the NHS, so it helps to take it early.
entries.note: Summary quoting NHS: start to work within two days.

entries.sentence: A single flare usually settles by itself, but almost everyone with gout has further flares, usually within a year.
entries.note: NHS: attack lasts 1 to 2 weeks untreated; NHS inform per summary: further flares usually within a year.

entries.note: Summary: NICE lifelong condition, long-term ULT.

entries.note: NHS: see a GP if usual treatments not helping.

entries.note: Summary: level often falls during a flare; NICE says can read lower.

entries.note: Summary quoting NHS-affiliated text: wait 4 weeks.

entries.note: Summary of NICE.

entries.note: Summary: spread units across the week.

entries.note: NHS: fever could mean joint infection.

entries.sentence: A first-time episode of gout symptoms should be seen by a GP.
entries.note: NHS: see a GP for symptoms of gout for the first time.

entries.note: NHS: 1 to 2 weeks if untreated.

entries.note: Summary: usual sites.

entries.note: Summary: NICE NSAID or steroid first line; NIAMS colchicine.

entries.note: Summary: lifelong condition, long-term ULT; lifelong treatment usually required.

entries.note: Summary: urate falls in a flare; GP may wait 4 weeks.

entries.note: Summary of VA and NHS lifestyle advice.
